 Nicola Coughlan “Will Not Be Watching” HBO’s ‘Harry Potter’: “And I Would Never Be in It”
 "I know people involved in those shows, and they’re nice people and whatever, but it’s not for me," said the 'Bridgerton' star, who has previously confronted author J.K. Rowling over her transphobia.

 Nicola Coughlan won’t be watching HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter series.
 The Bridgerton star sat down with British outlet The Observer to discuss her latest role in Channel 4’s I Am Helen , the next installment of Dominic Savage’s BAFTA-winning anthology series set to hit U.K. screens on Monday.
 Published over the weekend, the interview sees the Derry Girls alum talk about her charity work and vocal support for Palestinian causes amid the ongoing Israel-Gaza war, including her raising over two million pounds ($2.6m) for Palestine while doing press for the Netflix Regency era behemoth.

 She also, Rebecca Nicholson writes, marched for the legalization of abortion in her native Ireland and has consistently championed transgender rights. And last year, Coughlan was caught up in an online feud with Harry Potter author J.K. Rowling when the latter cheered on the U.K. Supreme Court’s ruling on the legal definition of women, which declared it to be based on biological sex. Rowling responded to Coughlan at the time claiming that she did not know who Coughlan was, nor fellow critic Pedro Pascal.
 “Me, I could believe,” Coughlan told The Observer . “But Pedro Pascal? You know who Pedro Pascal is, girl. Like, please.”
 Coughlan said she “loved” the Harry Potter books when she was younger. “But I will not be watching the new Harry Potter show and I would never be in it,” she added. “Look, I know people that are involved in those shows, and they’re nice people and whatever, but it’s not for me.”
 Potter author Rowling, a staunch advocate for anti-trans policies in Britain, has regularly come under fire for her transphobia. She has often been publicly criticized over her politics and creation of The J.K. Rowling Women’s Fund, a legal fund for individuals pushing anti-transgender views across the country.
 The controversy has been renewed by the TV series, with stars John Lithgow (playing Albus Dumbledore), Nick Frost (Rubeus Hagrid) and Bel Powley (Petunia Dursley) among the castmembers distancing themselves from Rowling’s views. She serves as an executive producer on the series, which hits HBO Max Dec. 25.
 “I find it ironic and somewhat inexplicable that Rowling has expressed such views,” said Lithgow earlier this year. “I’ve read about them, and I’ve never met her. She’s not really involved in this production at all. The people who are readapting Harry Potter and turning it into an eight-year-long TV series are remarkable. … These are people I really want to work with.”
 Coughlan said to The Observer that she credits her openness about her personal politics to seeing her parents “helping out, or being charitable, and not making a big deal of it.” With such a large social media following, she wanted to use that profile for the greater good. “In reality, people actually can help and make a difference. Six million followers is loads. But people have hundreds of millions. If you had 20 million, how much money could you raise?” she asked.
 She admitted to feeling disappointed when other celebrities “with those bigger platforms” didn’t “follow her into action.” Coughlan continues: “I had interesting conversations with certain people who said to me, ‘I’m not in a strong enough position,’ or ‘I don’t get to say anything, because my career is not as good’, or ‘I have too much to lose.’ And I thought, this is bullshit, isn’t it? Everyone has something to lose and everyone has something to gain. […] I just think I would never forgive myself if I didn’t say, ‘I think this is really fucking wrong,’ and I have a platform, and I want to try and do something practical, and that’s to raise money.”
